boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's battle at Jena on 14 October 1806 in cohort v1's fourth-coalition 1806 group: Napoleon's arrival on the Landgrafenberg and the night of 13-14 October, Marshal Lannes's attack on General Tauentzien's detachment, General Holtzendorf's fight on the Prussian left, Prince Hohenlohe's advance on Vierzehnheiligen and its defeat, General Rüchel's attack from Kapellendorf, and the losses. Marshal Davout's battle at Auerstedt the same day is a separate entry (B373a), as are Saalfeld (B371b) and the capitulation of Erfurt (B373b); the 5th Bulletin's results and French loss cover both fields of the 14th. Side A is the French. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) under Napoleon I 72 battalions with 83,500 infantry, 75 squadrons with 12,500 cavalry and 108 guns, 96,000 men in all, of whom 54,000 came into action, and side B (Prussians and Saxons) under General of Infantry Prince Hohenlohe 64 battalions with 42,500 infantry, 97 squadrons with 11,500 cavalry and 175 guns, 54,000 men in all, of whom 17,000 were Saxons. By his stated rule his strengths are the forces available for the battle, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed table and notes, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. His side A agrees closely with Foucart's three tables of the troops the Emperor had at the start of the day, about 11 o'clock and about noon (claim foucart-side-a): his 75 squadrons equal their 30 and 45 (our arithmetic), and his 83,500 infantry, 12,500 cavalry and 96,000 in all are near their 83,600 men, 12,300 horses and 95,900 (our arithmetic), but his 72 battalions are 10 fewer than their 82 (our arithmetic). His 54,000 in action is near Foucart's 50,600 men and 5,000 horses at the start of the day, 55,600 (our arithmetic). His side B is near Höpfner's 'some 50,000' Prussians and Saxons (claim hoepfner-side-b) and the 40,000 for Hohenlohe and 15,000 for Rüchel in Lieutenant-Colonel von der Goltz's account, 55,000 (our arithmetic); Foucart's own estimates, 44,000 and 28,000 (72,000, our arithmetic), include the Duke of Weimar's advanced guard, which was not at the battle (claim foucart-side-b). The passages read do not show his source for the 17,000 Saxons. The figures are forces available, which the commanders' dispositions shaped, so the phase is unresolved. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the entry: '1806 14 October: battle at Jena (1.)'; 'French | Prussians and Saxons'; 'Napoleon I. | General of Infantry Prince Hohenlohe'; '72 battalions 83,500 | infantry | 42,500 battalions 64'; '75 squadrons 12,500 | cavalry | 11,500 squadrons 97'; '108 guns 96,000 [1] | total strength | 54,000 [3] guns 175'. Notes: '[1] of these 54,000 men came into action'; '[3] of these Saxons: 17,000 men'. 'Btln.' is Bataillon, 'Esk.' Eskadron, 'Gesch.' Geschütze, 'Gen. d. Inf.' General der Infanterie, 'Fst.' Fürst and 'M.' Mann in Bodart's list of abbreviations.

claims.value: Side A in Foucart's tables: at the start of the day the Emperor had 50 battalions, 50,600 men, 30 squadrons and 5,000 horses: 17 battalions, 15,500 men, 6 squadrons and 1,000 horses of the 7th corps; 20, 19,000, 9 and 1,500 of the 5th corps; 5,000 men of the Imperial Guard on foot; 8, 7,700, 9 and 1,400 of the 1st division of the 4th corps; and 5, 3,400, 6 and 1,100 of the advanced guard of the 6th corps. About 11 o'clock there were in reserve on the plateau in the centre 14 battalions and 15,000 men of the 2nd and 3rd divisions of the 6th corps and 45 squadrons and 7,300 horses of the divisions d'Hautpoul, Klein and Nansouty, and about noon on the plateau on the right wing 18 battalions and 18,000 men of the 2nd and 3rd divisions of the 4th corps. Foucart adds that the 2 divisions of the 6th corps, the 2nd and 3rd divisions of the 4th corps, the Guard and the division Nansouty were not engaged, though present at the battle. The 5th Bulletin says that Marshal Ney had only a corps of 3,000 men, the only troops of his corps that had arrived, that the heavy cavalry, not yet with the army, could rejoin it only at noon, and that the cavalry of the Imperial Guard was 36 hours away.
claims.rationale: Foucart's tables (p. 671) and comment (p. 670) and the Bulletin (pp. 614, 615 and 617), read from the page images; each printed total of the tables equals the sum of its rows. The three tables together make 82 battalions, 83,600 men, 75 squadrons and 12,300 horses, 95,900 in all (our arithmetic), against Bodart's 72 battalions, 83,500 infantry, 75 squadrons and 12,500 cavalry, 96,000 in all (claim bodart-strength). The Bulletin's 3,000 men for Ney are fewer than the table's 3,400 men and 1,100 horses of the advanced guard of the 6th corps, 4,500 (our arithmetic). Foucart's tables count the troops on the field, not those that fought: by his comment the two divisions of the 6th corps, the two of the 4th, the Guard and the division Nansouty were present but not engaged. Which French troops were present followed from the orders of the 13th and the marches of the night (claim napoleon-decision), so the phase is unresolved. claims.value: Side A in Höpfner: the passages read give no count of the French army at Jena. The Guard infantry under Marshal Lefebvre formed a square on the summit of the Landgrafenberg on its arrival, and Napoleon bivouacked in its midst; Marshal Ney took his advanced guard up the height without waiting for the assembly of his whole corps, to take part in the battle early, while Marshal Soult's other divisions, like Ney's, could not reach the field before noon, and the heavy cavalry was not expected before noon. Höpfner judges that a lasting success was no longer possible for Prince Hohenlohe's advance, since on any further advance the Prussians already had to deal with a French force, its size read only in the OCR, that could be reinforced at any moment (all OCR so far). In his summary the some 50,000 Prussians and Saxons were overwhelmed by an enemy many times superior.
claims.rationale: Höpfner's narrative from the OCR, with his summary from the page image (p. 426). He gives no total for the French at Jena; his 'many times superior' enemy is not a count, and his figures for the Guard infantry and for the French force at the time of the prince's advance are read only in the OCR (not restated). Foucart's tables (claim foucart-side-a) and Bodart (claim bodart-strength) give the French present. The French troops on the field at each hour followed from the orders of the 13th and the night marches (claim napoleon-decision), so the phase is unresolved. English renderings (ours): 'the ... men of Guard infantry under Marshal Lefebvre formed, on their arrival, a square behind the centre on the summit of the Landgrafenberg, in whose midst Napoleon set up his bivouac'; 'the heavy cavalry could not be expected before noon of the ...' (OCR); '[Marshal Ney] would not wait for the assembly of the whole corps, but as soon as he had arrived with the advanced guard at the defiles to the Landgrafenberg and to Kospoda, he went up the height with it at once, in order to be able to take part in the battle early'; 'in the same way Marshal Soult had set in motion again, before daybreak, the light cavalry marching at the head of his corps and the division St. Hilaire; the ... other divisions, like those of Marshal Ney, could not reach the battlefield before noon'; 'a lasting [success] was no longer possible, since at this time, on further advance, one already had to deal with about ... men, who could receive reinforcement at any moment' (OCR); 'that was the end of the battle at Jena, in which some 50,000 Prussians and Saxons, in consequence of preceding mistakes, were led against the enemy little by little in a fight of several hours in such a way that the other detachments could not be taken in by those following until they had been completely overwhelmed by the many times superior enemy and put to flight' (p. 426).

claims.value: Side B in the documents Foucart prints: the 5th Bulletin has the Prussian army present itself in battle between Capellendorf and Auerstädt on the 13th nearly 150,000 strong, and on the 14th a corps of 50,000 men from its left move to cover the defiles of Naumburg while the two other corps, 80,000 men, advanced before the French army as it debouched from the plateau of Jena; Foucart notes that these are only general indications. A later Bulletin of the Grande Armée, on the situation of the Prussian army, composes Prince Hohenlohe's corps of 24 Prussian and 25 Saxon battalions, 45 Prussian and 36 Saxon squadrons, 2 artillery battalions and 8 Prussian and 8 Saxon batteries, and puts the Prussian forces at the battle of the 14th, without the Duke of Weimar's corps, still near Eisenach, and the Prince of Württemberg's reserve, at 126,000 men. Counting battalions at 700 men and squadrons at about 120 horses, Foucart estimates Rüchel's corps at 23,000 infantry and 5,000 horses, 28,000 men, including the Duke of Weimar's advanced guard, and Hohenlohe's at 34,000 infantry and 10,000 horses, 44,000 men, including Prince Louis's advanced guard and General Tauentzien's corps. In Lieutenant-Colonel von der Goltz's account, which Foucart quotes and which does not count the Duke of Weimar's advanced guard, General Rüchel with 15,000 men was to hold Weimar while Prince Hohenlohe with 40,000 occupied the plateau of Jena.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 612, 613, 614, 615 and 617), with Foucart's title and the later Bulletin's heading from the OCR (p. 611); by the transcription notes the composition and the 126,000 are the Bulletin's text and the estimates Foucart's, set in smaller type after it. The 5th Bulletin's 150,000 and 50,000 and the later Bulletin's 126,000 are for the whole army on both fields, Auerstedt included (B373a); the 5th Bulletin's 80,000 for the two corps before Jena is above every other figure. Foucart's estimates for Hohenlohe's and Rüchel's corps make 72,000 (our arithmetic) but include the Duke of Weimar's advanced guard, which the later Bulletin places away from the battle, near Eisenach; Goltz's 40,000 and 15,000 make 55,000 (our arithmetic), near Bodart's 54,000 (claim bodart-strength) and Höpfner's 'some 50,000' (claim hoepfner-side-b). Which troops fought followed the Prussian dispositions (claims side-b-command and side-b-objectives), so the phase is unresolved. English renderings (ours): the Bulletin, '5th Bulletin of the Grande Armée'; 'Iéna, 15 October 1806' (p. 614); 'and, on the 13th, it presented itself in battle between Capellendorf and Auerstädt, nearly 150,000 men strong' (p. 615); 'a corps of 50,000 men of the left moved to cover the defiles of Naumburg and seize the debouches of Kösen; but it had already been forestalled by Marshal Davout'; 'the two other corps, forming a force of 80,000 men, moved forward before the French army, which was debouching from the plateau of Iéna'; Foucart's note, 'these indications on the Prussian army are only general indications' (p. 617); Foucart's title, 'situation of the Prussian army', and the later Bulletin's heading, 'Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, ... November ...' (OCR); 'the corps of the Prince of Hohenlohe was composed of 24 Prussian battalions and 25 Saxon battalions, of 45 Prussian squadrons and 36 Saxon squadrons, of 2 battalions of artillery, of 8 Prussian batteries and 8 Saxon batteries'; 'this whole army was at the battle of the 14th, except the corps of the Duke of Weimar, which was still near Eisenach, and the reserve of the Prince of Württemberg; which brings the Prussian forces that were at the battle to 126,000 men'; Foucart, 'counting the battalions at 700 men and the squadrons at about 120 horses, one may estimate:'; 'the corps of Rüchel at 23,000 men of infantry and 5,000 horses, that is 28,000 men, including the advanced guard of the Duke of Weimar;' (p. 612); 'the corps of Hohenlohe at 34,000 men of infantry and 10,000 horses, that is 44,000 men, including the advanced guard of Prince Louis and the corps of General Tauenzien;'; 'the strengths given by Lieutenant-Colonel von der Goltz are very nearly the same; he does not count the advanced guard of the Duke of Weimar'; Goltz, '« ...the Prussian army, says this senior officer, after the loss of the bridge of Naumburg, had at last decided to break toward its left in order to keep to its lines of communication'; 'General Rüchel with 15,000 men was to hold at Weimar, while Prince Hohenlohe with 40,000 men occupied the plateau of Iéna and covered the army's march toward the left' (p. 613).

claims.value: Side A's command: Napoleon commanded in person. Late in the night he examined the ground with Marshals Lannes and Soult and General Suchet, and on his return issued the disposition for the battle (OCR). In Höpfner's German text of that order Marshal Augereau commanded the left wing and Lannes the centre, occupying the plateau of Jena where it opens toward the plain, and the village before the right wing (Closwitz) was to be fired on by the whole artillery of the division Suchet and immediately attacked and taken (OCR); in the 5th Bulletin the left of the French army, resting on a village and woods, was commanded by Augereau, the Imperial Guard separated it from the centre held by Lannes's corps, and the right was formed by Marshal Soult's corps. In General Suchet's report Lannes ordered him to move the brigade Claparède to the left, and the Emperor in person disposed of the brigade Vedel and put it in support of the division Desjardins; Foucart notes, from Suchet's report, that the Emperor himself ordered the second attack of the centre, on Vierzehnheiligen (OCR). Marshal Ney, in Höpfner, would not wait for his whole corps and took his advanced guard up the height to take part early; on his order General Colbert charged a Prussian battery in the flank, and he then held his ground between Vierzehnheiligen and the forest to keep the Prussians from taking the offensive before Augereau's corps arrived (OCR). Napoleon, by Höpfner's account, deliberately confined himself to the defensive at Vierzehnheiligen until he saw Augereau's division Desjardins debouch and Soult's troops available, then directed Desjardins on Isserstedt with Lannes's brigade Wedell in support (OCR); in the Bulletin the Emperor always kept near him, besides the Imperial Guard, a good number of reserve troops, and all the troops in reserve were then brought up to the first line, which overthrew the enemy (OCR).

Napoleon's disposition, his handling of the reserves and his direction of the attacks were his own decisions on the field, as were Ney's early engagement and Lannes's orders to Suchet, so the claim is tagged commander_created. Höpfner gives the disposition in German as Napoleon's order, without naming its source in the passages read. The Bulletin has battalions engaged at Hohlstedt and Lannes ordered to support that village; Foucart's note, from Suchet's report, puts the second attack of the centre on Vierzehnheiligen, not Hohlstedt (claim posture). claims.value: Side B's command: by Höpfner's reflections the main army marched off and Prince Hohenlohe was to cover the right flank of its march and then follow (OCR). On the morning of the battle General Zeschwitz, asking for instructions, was answered that the troops should be ready to march out but not tired uselessly, and the prince ordered General Müffling that the battalions should stay quietly in camp until the fog lifted, nothing serious being expected that day. General Grawert, to whom nothing seemed more necessary than to turn his division's front toward the enemy, begged the prince most urgently to let the movement he had begun be completed, and the prince, though it was disagreeable to him, at last consented; Grawert had asked Colonel Massenbach to take General Tauentzien back to Vierzehnheiligen and was answered that 'the hole at Jena' must not be lost. The prince wrote to General Rüchel that he was being violently attacked and asked for whatever Prussian troops could be spared, ordered the infantry to advance once it had completed its alignment, and sent General Holtzendorf the order to march at once against the enemy's right flank, but its bearer took the long detour by Hermstedt and could no longer carry it out in time. In the opening fight, against Lannes's corps, the prince's order to withdraw, form the troops at Kl. Romstedt and draw fresh ammunition there came only at a critical moment, when the ammunition was spent, and he told the retreating troops that nothing was lost and he would renew the attack at once. With his corps's reserve gone, he halted Grawert's infantry to let the fog lift and the enemy come further into the plain, then ordered an advance in echelons from the left wing, and halted again before the village; he resolved to take it with the bayonet, but gave way to Grawert, who urged him to hold the position until Rüchel's corps arrived. A favourable moment that remained to begin the retreat on Rüchel's corps together with the Saxons was missed, and the prince still counted on Rüchel's arrival and hoped with his help to hold the field at least for the rest of the day (all OCR so far). General Holtzendorf chose, of the ways open to him, to open his connection with the prince by force, and attacked in battalion echelons from his right wing (OCR). General Rüchel, ordered to serve as a rallying point for the Duke of Weimar but wishing to support the prince or the main army as needed, was summoned by a courier from the King to march on Auerstedt, but judged that he would arrive there too late and might still help the prince; Colonel Massenbach told him he could help 'now only through Kapellendorf', and Rüchel attacked from there after offering the prince the command (OCR).
claims.rationale: Höpfner's narrative and reflections, from the OCR. Hohenlohe's task was set by the Duke's orders (claim side-b-objectives); his handling of the battle, the halts, the advance in echelons and the choice to wait for Rüchel, and Rüchel's decision to march to his help and attack from Kapellendorf, were the commanders' own, so the claim is tagged commander_created. In Höpfner's summary the some 50,000 Prussians and Saxons were led against the enemy little by little in consequence of preceding mistakes (claim hoepfner-side-a). claims.value: Napoleon's decision: in the 5th Bulletin the Emperor arrived at Jena at two in the afternoon of the 13th and, from a small plateau held by the advanced guard, saw the enemy's dispositions: the enemy seemed to be manoeuvring to attack the next day and force the debouches of the Saale, and defended the road from Jena to Weimar in force and in an impregnable position. Though the heavy cavalry could rejoin only at noon and the Guard cavalry was 36 hours away, 'there are moments in war when no consideration must outweigh the advantage of forestalling the enemy and attacking him first': the Emperor had Lannes's whole corps drawn up on the plateau, which the enemy seemed to have neglected, had a road worked in the rock all night to bring the artillery up, and ordered Davout to debouch by Naumburg, to defend the defiles of Kösen or to go to Apolda and take the enemy in the rear, while Bernadotte's corps was to debouch from Dornburg and fall on the enemy's rear. In the position he had taken after the morning's attack the Emperor would have liked to delay coming to blows by two hours, to await the troops that were to join him and above all his cavalry, but French ardour carried the day (the last words OCR). In Höpfner, Lannes, who had posted his advanced guard on the Landgrafenberg, reported that he faced considerable forces, about 50,000 men, and feared attack before evening; Napoleon, not doubting that the united Prussian force stood opposite Lannes, decided at once to profit from the marshal's cheap gain of the position before the opponent recognised his mistake, and recognised the importance of the post on the Landgrafenberg, which secured his debouch onto the plateau and hid his attack movements from the Prussians (the last OCR); resolved to attack the Prussian army between Jena and Weimar, he called on Davout to march on Apolda to act in its rear.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 614, 615, 617, 355 and 365), with the end of the Bulletin's sentence and Höpfner's account of the post from the OCR. The decision to attack from the Landgrafenberg, before his cavalry and all his corps had come up, was Napoleon's own, so the claim is tagged commander_created; Lannes's possession of the Landgrafenberg, which Höpfner calls cheaply gained, set the opportunity (claim jena-ground). Höpfner and Colonel Blein, quoted by Foucart, agree that Napoleon believed the united Prussian force, or the King's army, to be before him (claim side-a-information). English renderings (ours): the Bulletin, '5th Bulletin of the Grande Armée'; 'Iéna, 15 October 1806' (p. 614); 'on the 13th, at two o'clock in the afternoon, the Emperor arrived at Iéna, and, on a small plateau occupied by our advanced guard, he perceived the dispositions of the enemy, who seemed to be manoeuvring to attack the next day and force the various debouches of the Saale'; 'the enemy defended in force and by an impregnable position the road from Iéna to Weimar, and seemed to think that the French could not debouch into the plain without having forced this passage'; as in claim foucart-side-a for the cavalry; 'but there are moments in war when no consideration must outweigh the advantage of forestalling the enemy and attacking him first'; 'the Emperor had the whole corps of Marshal Lannes drawn up on the plateau occupied by the advanced guard, which the enemy seemed to have neglected and opposite which he was in position'; 'all night work was done on a road in the rock, and the artillery was successfully brought onto the height'; 'Marshal Davout received the order to debouch by Naumburg, to defend the defiles of Kösen if the enemy wished to march on Naumburg, or to go to Apolda to take him in the rear if he remained in the position where he was'; 'the corps of the Marshal Prince of Ponte-Corvo was destined to debouch from Dornburg to fall on the enemy's rear, whether he moved in force on Naumburg or on Iéna' (p. 615); 'the Emperor would have wished to delay coming to blows by two hours, in order to await, in the position he had just taken after the morning's attack, the troops that were to join him and above all his cavalry; but the ardour' (p. 617); '[French ardour] carried the day' (OCR); Höpfner, as in claim hoepfner-side-b for Lannes's report (p. 355); 'he did not doubt that the united Prussian force stood in the fine position on the plateau between Saale and Ilm opposite Marshal Lannes, and decided at once to draw advantage from the favourable possession that the marshal had taken so cheaply, before the opponent recognised his mistake' (p. 355); '[he] very soon recognised the importance of the post on the Landgrafenberg, which secured him the debouch onto the plateau and withdrew the attack movements from the eyes of the Prussians' (OCR); 'according to them Napoleon, who was resolved to attack the Prussian army between Jena and Weimar, called on the marshal to direct himself on Apolda, in order to act in the rear of the Prussian army, leaving to him the road he would take for it' (p. 365).

claims.value: Bodart codes the battle at Jena on 14 October 1806 as a victory of the French under Napoleon I over the Prussians and Saxons under Prince Hohenlohe: by his rule the winner stands on the left. In Höpfner the some 50,000 Prussians and Saxons were led against the enemy little by little, so that each body was completely overwhelmed by the many times superior enemy and put to flight before the next could take it up; in the 5th Bulletin the French first line, supported by the reserves, overthrew the enemy and put him in full retreat (OCR).

claims.value: Bodart gives the French losses as 6·3% = about 6,000 killed and wounded (6 generals, 39 staff officers, 288 officers), in all about 6,000 (333 officers), which he notes is 11·0% of the troops that had been in action; and the Prussian-Saxon losses as about 12,000 killed and wounded (9 generals, 46 staff officers, 257 officers) = 22·3% and 15,000 prisoners = 27·7%, in all about 27,000 = 50·0%, with 112 cannon (= 65%). By his note the Prussian-Saxon losses in men come from French sources (Martin, Histoire de France), since on the Prussian side the men's losses could not be established because of the army's complete dissolution after the battle. He gives the Saxon losses as 1,200 men (1 general, 15 staff officers, 98 'Ob.-Offz.') killed and wounded and 6,000 prisoners, together 7,200 men, and prints a dagger before the Prussian Major-General von Schönermark, which we read as marking him fallen (our reading; claim bodart-commanders).
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed losses, read from the page image in the frame transcription, compared with Höpfner's officers' losses from the page images (pp. 426 and 427). His French 6,000 is 6·3% of his 96,000 (our arithmetic, 6·25%) and 11·1% of his 54,000 in action (our arithmetic), against his printed 11·0%; his 6 generals, 39 staff officers and 288 officers make 333 (our arithmetic), as printed. For side B his 12,000 and 15,000 are 22·2% and 27·8% of his 54,000 (our arithmetic), against his printed 22·3% and 27·7%, and his 27,000 is 50·0%, as printed; his 112 cannon are 64% of his 175 guns (our arithmetic), not the printed 65%. His 9 generals, 46 staff officers and 257 officers make 312 (our arithmetic), the same as Höpfner's 49 officers killed or dead of wounds and 263 wounded (our arithmetic); his 9 generals equal Höpfner's 8 Prussian and 1 Saxon wounded generals, and his 46 staff officers Höpfner's 10 and 4 killed and 21 and 11 wounded (our arithmetic). His Saxon officers, 1 general, 15 staff officers and 98 'Ob.-Offz.', make 114, the same as Höpfner's 19 Saxon officers killed and 95 wounded, and his 15 Saxon staff officers equal Höpfner's 4 killed and 11 wounded (our arithmetic). His 112 cannon are far more than Höpfner's 24 Prussian guns lost without the battalion guns, Höpfner adding that the Saxon loss in guns could not be determined, though few may have escaped (claim side-b-losses-reported). The passages read do not show his source for the French losses. claims.value: Side A's losses as reported: the 5th Bulletin, whose account of the battle includes Marshal Davout's action on the right, which held and drove back the bulk of the enemy troops that were to debouch toward Kösen, estimates the French loss at 1,000 or 1,100 killed and 3,000 wounded, and among the generals regrets only General Debilly. General Suchet's report to Marshal Lannes, dated Weimar 15 October 1806, puts the total loss in killed or wounded at 2,645, among them 75 officers; the sentence before it gives the rounds his artillery fired at Saalfeld and at the battle of Iéna together, 1,322; after Saalfeld he had put his loss at 172 men out of action and 10 horses killed. Höpfner says the French loss must have been very considerable, but that no credible figure is found anywhere.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 614, 619, 620, 632, 635, 474 and 427), with the heading of Suchet's report on Saalfeld from the OCR. The Bulletin tells the day as one battle, with Davout's action at Auerstedt (B373a) on its right, so its loss figure is read as covering both fields; the passages read do not divide it between them. Suchet's figure is for his division; whether it includes the 172 of Saalfeld is not stated: the artillery sentence before it covers both actions, and if the total does include Saalfeld, the loss at Jena would be 2,473 (our arithmetic). Bodart's about 6,000 with 333 officers (claim bodart-losses) has no source in the passages read. No French return for the army at Jena was found (open questions). English renderings (ours): the Bulletin, '5th Bulletin of the Grande Armée'; 'Iéna, 15 October 1806' (p. 614); 'on our right the corps of Marshal Davout performed prodigies; not only did he contain, but he drove back, for more than 3 leagues, the bulk of the enemy troops that were to debouch toward Kösen' (p. 619); 'on our side we have to regret, among the generals, only the loss of General Debilly, an excellent soldier'; 'our loss is estimated at 1,000 or 1,100 killed and 3,000 wounded' (p. 620); Suchet, 'General Suchet to Marshal Lannes'; 'Weimar, 15 October 1806' (p. 632); 'the artillery fired at Saalfeld and at the battle of Iéna 1,322 rounds of cannon'; 'the total loss in killed or wounded amounts to 2,645, among whom 75 officers' (p. 635); his report on Saalfeld, 'report of General Suchet on the combat of Saalfeld' (OCR); 'my loss amounts to 172 men out of action and 10 horses killed' (p. 474); Höpfner, 'the loss of the French must have been very considerable, but nowhere is a credible figure found' (p. 427).

claims.value: Side B's losses as reported: the 5th Bulletin gives as the results of the battle 30,000 to 40,000 prisoners, with more arriving every moment, 25 to 30 colours, 300 pieces of cannon and immense magazines of subsistence; among the prisoners more than 20 generals, several of them lieutenant-generals, among them Lieutenant-General Schmettau; and more than 20,000 killed or wounded in the Prussian army. Höpfner holds a statement of the allies' loss quite impossible, since the units dissolved after the battle, but infers the men's loss from the officers': 30 Prussian and 19 Saxon officers, 49 in all, were killed or died of wounds, among them 10 Prussian and 4 Saxon staff officers, and 168 Prussian officers, without the general staff and adjutants, and 95 Saxon officers, 263 in all, were wounded, among them 8 generals and 21 staff officers of the Prussians and 1 general and 11 staff officers of the Saxons; he thinks the Prussian figure for the wounded may well be taken as approximately correct. 24 Prussian guns were lost, without the battalion guns; the Saxon loss in guns could not be determined, but few may have escaped. For single units he gives the losses of the regiment of Gettkandt hussars and of the regiment Winning (OCR, not restated).
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 614, 619, 620, 426 and 427), with Höpfner's figures for single units from the OCR. The Bulletin's results are likewise read as covering both fields, Jena and Auerstedt (B373a) (claim side-a-losses-reported). Höpfner's officers' losses equal Bodart's (claim bodart-losses); his 24 Prussian guns, without the battalion guns and the Saxon guns, are far fewer than Bodart's 112 cannon and the Bulletin's 300 pieces. By Bodart's note his men's losses for side B come from French sources (claim bodart-losses). claims.value: Jena is a town in Saxe-Weimar, 20 km south-east of Weimar (Bodart). In the 5th Bulletin the enemy defended the road from Jena to Weimar in force and by an impregnable position, and seemed to think the French could not debouch into the plain without forcing that passage; it did not seem possible to bring artillery up onto the plateau held by the advanced guard, which was so small that four battalions could scarcely deploy on it, and a road was worked in the rock all night to bring the artillery up; it was perhaps the first time an army had to pass through so small a debouch (the last OCR). In Höpfner the post on the Landgrafenberg secured Napoleon's debouch onto the plateau and hid his attack movements from the Prussians, and the French artillery was brought up by the Steiger and the ravine of Kospoda, whose ascents were levelled and widened as far as could be done in the night (OCR). A thick, cold fog lay on the height and long hid everything but what was near, which, Höpfner says, must have greatly favoured the superior attacker in the difficult moment of deploying from the deep formation into the plain still to be won (OCR); in the Bulletin the fog covered both armies for two hours, then lifted under a fine autumn sun, and the two armies saw each other at short cannon range. In the fog the French skirmishers could advance only uncertainly, and for want of a point of direction, since Closwitz could not be seen, the attackers followed the natural fall of the ground and were led too far left (Höpfner, OCR); in General Suchet's report the fog scarcely let objects be made out a few paces off, and all the corps of his division were thrown strongly to the left as if dragged by the slope of the ground (OCR). The left of the French army rested on a village and woods (the Bulletin). At Vierzehnheiligen the French held behind houses and barns, and when they left the front houses they held, as before, behind the garden enclosures (OCR). In Lieutenant-Colonel von der Goltz's account, quoted by Foucart, the main body of the army camped between Capellendorf and the Schnecke facing south-west, though the French were known to be on the right bank of the Saale, so that the troops had first to be faced about to leave the camp. General Holtzendorf's ground was unknown to him, narrow and set with hollows and dense thickets, and in the retreat some of the Prussian guns, cumbersome and drawn by wretched horses, could be moved only with difficulty through ploughed land and potato fields (OCR).
claims.rationale: Bodart's place note, read from the page image in the frame transcription; the Bulletin (pp. 615 and 617), Suchet's heading (p. 632) and Goltz (p. 613) from the page images; the rest from the OCR. The ground and the weather were there before the battle, so the claim is inherited; the use of the Landgrafenberg and the road in the rock were Napoleon's (claim napoleon-decision), and the camp's facing the Prussian command's (claim side-b-command). The paragraph on the camp continues the quotation from Goltz opened on the same page ('says this senior officer'), the print opening each paragraph of the quotation with a guillemet and closing it only at its end. English renderings (ours): Bodart, '(town in Germany, Saxe-Weimar, 20 km south-east of Weimar)'; the Bulletin, as in claim foucart-side-a for the heading and date (p. 614); as in claim napoleon-decision for the road from Jena to Weimar and the road in the rock; 'it did not seem possible, in fact, to bring artillery up onto the plateau, which, moreover, was so small that four battalions could scarcely deploy on it' (p. 615); 'for it was perhaps the first time that an army had to pass through so small a debouch' (OCR); Höpfner, as in claim napoleon-decision for the post (OCR); 'the rest of the ... and the night to the ... were used to bring the artillery of the ... corps and of the Guard by the Steiger and the ravine of Kospoda onto the plateau, and'; 'for this these ascents were levelled and widened as far as could be done in the night'; 'a thick, cold fog lay on the height and for a long time hid all objects except at near distances, a circumstance that must have been of uncommon advantage to the superior attacker in the most difficult moment of the deployment from the deep formation into the plain still to be won' (OCR); the Bulletin, 'the fog covered the two armies for two hours; but at last it was dispelled by a fine autumn sun'; 'the two armies perceived each other at short cannon range'; as in claim side-a-command for the left (p. 617); Höpfner, 'in the thick fog the French skirmishers could advance only uncertainly, and for want of a point of direction, since Kloswitz could not be seen, the attackers followed the natural fall of the ground and were thereby led too far to the left' (OCR); Suchet, as in claim side-a-losses-reported for the heading and date (p. 632); '[the thick fog that] envelops [us] scarcely allows objects to be made out a few paces away'; 'all the corps of the division, which the advance had pressed together, were strongly thrown to the left and as if dragged by the slope of the ground on which we found ourselves' (OCR); Höpfner, as in claim fortification for the houses and gardens (OCR); Goltz, as in claim foucart-side-b for the quotation's opening; 'the main body of the army camped between Capellendorf and the Schnecke and, although it was already known that the French were on the right bank of the Saale, the army nonetheless faced south-west'; 'the result was that when the troops had to be led against the enemy, they first had to be faced to the rear to leave the camp...' (p. 613); Höpfner, 'the fog hid all objects, the ground was quite unknown to the general, narrow and set with hollows and dense thickets;'; 'the cumbersome ...-pounders could be moved only laboriously through the ploughed land and potato fields by the wretched horses harnessed to them' (OCR).

claims.value: Side A: in the 5th Bulletin it did not seem possible to bring artillery up onto the small plateau, and a road was worked in the rock all night to bring it onto the height; the heavy cavalry, not yet with the army, could rejoin it only at noon, and the cavalry of the Imperial Guard was 36 hours away. In Höpfner the ascents by the Steiger and the ravine of Kospoda were levelled and widened in the night to bring the French artillery up (OCR). Foucart notes that the whole mass of men and horses on the plateau spent the night in an extremely cramped bivouac, probably without water (OCR). On the field, in General Suchet's report one of his regiments lacked cartridges and was singularly weakened, and in Höpfner a French light regiment that had shot off its ammunition was relieved (OCR); Suchet's artillery fired 1,322 rounds at Saalfeld and at Jena together. Side B: in the opening fight the prince's order to withdraw and draw fresh ammunition came only when the ammunition was spent, the infantry of the brigade Dyherrn soon shot off its few cartridges, and in the retreat some of the Prussian guns, cumbersome and drawn by wretched horses, could be moved only with difficulty through ploughed land and potato fields (OCR). In Höpfner's reflections the army, in the rich country where it stood, could not bring itself to requisition and let men and horses go hungry (OCR).

No return of ammunition or supply on hand for either side was found in the passages read. claims.value: Side A's information: in the 5th Bulletin the Emperor, arriving at Jena, saw from the plateau the enemy's dispositions and judged that the enemy seemed to be manoeuvring to attack the next day; in Höpfner's version of his address to the troops the Prussian army was cut off like Mack's at Ulm and fought only to break through and regain its communications (OCR). In Höpfner, Lannes estimated the forces opposite him at about 50,000 men, and Napoleon did not doubt that the united Prussian force stood opposite Lannes; Davout and Bernadotte were to march on Apolda in the rear of the Prussian army between Jena and Weimar because Napoleon did not know that the greater part of it had marched off toward the Unstrut, and late in the night he examined the ground in person with Lannes, Soult and Suchet (OCR). Colonel Blein, quoted by Foucart, says the Emperor was uneasy all day about Davout's and Bernadotte's corps and saw well that he had not had to deal with the whole Prussian army, but believed that the King's army was before him. On the field the fog hid everything (claim jena-ground): in General Suchet's report the fire was opened in the darkness of the fog, which did not allow the enemy's strength to be judged, and in Höpfner Napoleon could survey the Prussian forces no better than Prince Hohenlohe could judge his, so that it was wise, Höpfner judges, to stake nothing on the uncertain when he knew he would shortly be the stronger in any case (OCR). Napoleon went back to Jena and received the news of the outcome of the battle at Auerstedt only late in the night.
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 614, 615, 619, 355 and 426) and the OCR as marked. Napoleon's belief that he faced the main Prussian army shaped his orders to Davout and Bernadotte (claim napoleon-decision), and what he learned on the field came partly from his own reconnaissance, so the phase is unresolved. Lannes's 50,000 is near Bodart's 54,000 for side B (claim bodart-strength); the Bulletin's 80,000 for the two corps before the French army (claim foucart-side-b) is above both. English renderings (ours): the Bulletin, as in claim napoleon-decision for the heading, date and plateau (pp. 614 and 615); Höpfner, 'the Prussian army is cut off like that of General Mack at Ulm a year ago today. This army now fights only to break through and regain its communications' (OCR); as in claims hoepfner-side-b and napoleon-decision for Lannes's report and Napoleon's conclusion (p. 355); 'the corps of Davout and Bernadotte were to march together the next morning on Apolda in the rear of the Prussian army between Jena and Weimar, since Napoleon did not know that the greater part of it had marched off toward the Unstrut'; 'late in the night Napoleon, accompanied only by Marshals Lannes and Soult and General Suchet, examined the ground, and when he had returned he issued the disposition for the battle' (OCR); Blein, '« ..... The Emperor, says Colonel Blein, was uneasy all day about the corps of Marshals Davout and Bernadotte'; 'he saw well that he had not had to deal with the whole Prussian army, but he believed that the King's army was before him..... »' (p. 619); Suchet, as in claim side-a-losses-reported for the heading and date (p. 632); 'from then on a sustained fire of musketry and artillery begins in the darkness of the fog, which did not allow the enemy's strength to be judged' (OCR); Höpfner, 'he could no more survey the forces of the Prussians adequately than Prince Hohenlohe had so far been able to judge his; it was therefore also wise to stake nothing on the uncertain, when he knew that he would in any case shortly be the superior' (OCR); 'Napoleon went back to Jena and received only late in the night the news of the outcome of the battle at Auerstädt' (p. 426).

claims.value: Side B's information: at midnight Rittmeister Derschau returned from General Tauentzien with the news that the enemy was reinforcing on the Landgrafenberg, that he had seen its movements and heard work on the roads to bring guns up the height; no special notice seems to have been taken of this; at least it was said that guns brought up the height must infallibly fall into Prussian hands. The rest of the night at Kapellendorf was slept away in complete ignorance of what the next day would bring: it was supposed that the French main masses would turn toward Leipzig and Naumburg, and believed that the Prussians would be occupied the next day only by feints (OCR). On the morning of the battle General Zeschwitz, asking for instructions, was answered that for several reasons it must be assumed there would be no serious fight that day, and the prince told General Müffling that nothing serious was to be expected; soon after, he wrote to General Rüchel that he was being violently attacked (OCR). Before Vierzehnheiligen the uncertainty about what was opposite him was among the reasons that made the prince halt; General Zeschwitz reported that from the Schnecke some enemy detachments could be seen going back, but several strong columns were advancing from Closwitz and Kospoda toward Vierzehnheiligen and the Isserstedt forest in support, and General Grawert had congratulated the prince on the battle won (OCR). In Höpfner's reflections, when the Duke forbade any serious engagement it was not known that the prince had given up the great Saale defiles (OCR).
claims.rationale: Höpfner's narrative and reflections, from the OCR. The prince's belief that no serious fight was coming shaped his orders on the morning of the battle (claim side-b-command), and the reports that reached him depended on his staff and subordinates, so the phase is unresolved. English renderings (ours): 'at midnight Rittmeister Derschau returned from General Count Tauentzien and brought the news that the enemy was reinforcing himself on the Landgrafenberg, that he himself had seen his movements and at the same time heard how work was being done on the roads to bring cannon up the height'; 'no special notice seems, however, to have been taken of these communications; at least it was said that cannon brought up the height must infallibly fall into Prussian hands'; 'the rest of the night was slept away at Kapellendorf in complete ignorance of what was in store on the following day;'; '[it was supposed that the French main] masses would turn toward Leipzig and Naumburg, and it was therefore believed that on the ... one would be occupied only by feints'; 'General Zeschwitz sent to ask for instructions,'; 'that the troops should hold themselves ready to march out, but that they should not be tired uselessly, because for several reasons it must be assumed that it would not yet come to a serious fight on this day'; 'the prince called General Müffling, who commanded the right-wing brigade, to him and ordered him,'; 'that the battalions should keep quiet in the camp until the fog had lifted, since nothing serious was to be expected for this day'; 'the prince had sent Lieutenant Förster of the Prittwitz dragoons from the camp to General Rüchel with the message written on the writing tablet:'; '„I am just now being violently attacked and have had the Prussian division march off to the left. I ask Your Excellency to send me of Prussian troops what you can spare.'; 'however, the sight of the single line without a particular reserve, the uncertainty about what one had opposite, the complete unfamiliarity with the means against the swarms of French skirmishers, the necessity of first taking Vierzehnheiligen, all this made the prince halt'; 'but then General Zeschwitz sent by Lieutenant Odeleben the report that from the Schnecke some enemy detachments could indeed be seen going back,'; 'that, on the other hand, several strong columns were approaching from Kloswitz and Kospoda toward Vierzehnheiligen and the Isserstedt forest in support'; 'then the prince, who may have thought only one last effort necessary, resolved to send a couple of battalions against Vierzehnheiligen and have it taken with the bayonet, when General Grawert came up to him and congratulated him on the battle won'; 'the Duke's prohibition of any serious engagement was justified; one wished to accept battle with united forces under more favourable strategic circumstances, and did not know that the prince had already given up the great Saale defiles without more ado' (OCR).

claims.value: Side A's objectives: in the 5th Bulletin the Emperor, seeing the enemy apparently preparing to attack the next day and force the debouches of the Saale, judged that nothing should outweigh the advantage of forestalling the enemy and attacking him first; Davout was to debouch by Naumburg, to defend the defiles of Kösen if the enemy marched on Naumburg or to go to Apolda and take him in the rear if he stayed in his position, and Bernadotte's corps was to debouch from Dornburg and fall on the enemy's rear. In Höpfner, Napoleon was resolved to attack the Prussian army between Jena and Weimar and called on Davout to march on Apolda to act in its rear; his disposition for the battle declared it important that day to deploy in the plain, the arrangements to be those the enemy's movements and forces prescribed, to drive him from the positions needed for the deployment, gave Lannes the centre and had Closwitz attacked and taken (OCR). Höpfner says that Napoleon had so far deliberately confined himself to the defensive at Vierzehnheiligen, and judges it wise of him to stake nothing on the uncertain when he knew he would shortly be the stronger in any case (OCR).
claims.rationale: Read from the page images (pp. 614, 615 and 365) and the OCR as marked. The objectives came partly from the campaign, in which Napoleon told his troops that the Prussian army was cut off (claim side-a-information), and partly from Napoleon's decisions on the evening and the morning of the battle (claim napoleon-decision), so the phase is unresolved. English renderings (ours): the Bulletin, as in claim napoleon-decision for the heading, date, plateau, forestalling, Davout and Bernadotte (pp. 614 and 615); Höpfner, as in claim napoleon-decision for the orders to Davout (p. 365); as in claim side-a-command for the order's opening, the centre and Kloswitz (OCR); 'it is important today to deploy in the plain. claims.value: Side B's objectives: by Höpfner's reflections the Duke did not wish to fight but to march off to the left, cross the Unstrut and place himself again directly before the French; the main army marched off, and Prince Hohenlohe was to cover the right flank of its march and then follow. The Duke's prohibition of any serious engagement was meant to accept battle later with united forces under more favourable strategic conditions; Höpfner holds that the prince could judge what the prohibition meant and had to drive the enemy's head back off the Landgrafenberg (OCR). In Lieutenant-Colonel von der Goltz's account, quoted by Foucart, the Prussian army had at last decided, after the loss of the bridge of Naumburg, to break toward its left to keep to its lines of communication, General Rüchel with 15,000 men was to hold at Weimar, and Prince Hohenlohe with 40,000 occupied the plateau of Jena and covered the army's march toward the left. In the 5th Bulletin the main body of the enemy army had planned to attack only when the fog had lifted. On the field General Grawert was told that 'the hole at Jena' must not be lost; the prince halted to let the enemy come further into the plain and give his cavalry room, chose on Grawert's advice to hold his position before Vierzehnheiligen until Rüchel's corps arrived and then take the village and complete the victory, and still hoped with Rüchel's help to hold the field for the rest of the day (OCR). General Rüchel, ordered to serve as a rallying point for the Duke of Weimar, wished also to be able to support the prince or the main army as needed, and when summoned by the King toward Auerstedt judged that he would arrive there too late but might still help the prince (OCR).
claims.rationale: Höpfner's narrative and reflections from the OCR; Goltz (p. 613) and the Bulletin (pp. 614 and 617) from the page images. The Duke's orders set Hohenlohe's task; the prince's reading of it, his halts and his choice to wait for Rüchel, and Rüchel's choice to march to his help, were their own (claim side-b-command), so the phase is unresolved. Höpfner's 'the Duke' is the Duke of Brunswick, who held the army command (his reflections). The Bulletin's statement of the Prussian plan is the enemy's. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'the Duke, however, did not want to fight; he wanted to march off to the left, to cross the Unstrut and to place himself again directly before the French'; 'the army command had been organised in a highly unsuitable way, in that the Duke of Brunswick was given a council at whose head the King himself stood, instead of leaving the Duke the whole responsibility;'; as in claim side-b-command for the march; as in claim side-b-information for the prohibition; 'but the prince could judge what the prohibition was meant to say; he had to drive the enemy's head back off the Landgrafenberg again and occupy Dornburg and Kamburg' [the OCR reads 'Dormburg und Hamburg'] (OCR); Goltz, as in claim foucart-side-b (p. 613); the Bulletin, as in claim foucart-side-a for the heading and date (p. 614); 'for its part, the main body of the enemy army, which had planned to attack only when the fog had cleared, took up arms' (p. 617); Höpfner, as in claim side-b-command for the hole at Jena, the halt, Grawert's advice, the prince's hope, Rüchel's orders, the King's courier and Rüchel's judgment (OCR).

claims.value: Both sides attacked. In Höpfner, Napoleon gave the order to attack early in the morning (the hour OCR), and at about the same time General Tauentzien ordered his troops to reoccupy the position they had held the evening before; through this advance on both sides the fighting parties soon ran into each other, and Lannes's corps threw back Tauentzien's detachment (OCR). Prince Hohenlohe then had General Grawert's infantry advance, and later advance in echelons from the left wing, against Vierzehnheiligen, where Napoleon had so far deliberately confined himself to the defensive with artillery and skirmisher fire; reinforced by Soult's and Augereau's troops, a division of Ney's corps and cavalry, the French renewed the attack, and the whole mass of fresh forces pressed forward; General Holtzendorf attacked in battalion echelons from his right wing, and General Rüchel's corps attacked from Kapellendorf toward the height, where new French lines outflanked and enfiladed it (OCR). In General Suchet's report his division formed at daybreak to seize the village of Closwitz. In the 5th Bulletin the French dislodged the enemy from his position and debouched into the plain, and the main body of the enemy army, which had planned to attack only when the fog had lifted, took up arms, two of its corps advancing before the French army as it debouched from the plateau; when the enemy moved to dislodge French battalions engaged at a village, Lannes was ordered to march in echelons to support it, and the French reserves were then brought up and overthrew the enemy (partly OCR).
claims.rationale: Coded both_attacked: the French attacked Tauentzien's detachment at dawn and later Hohenlohe's line, and Hohenlohe made a main attack of his own, advancing out of his camp against the French who had debouched onto the plateau, at Vierzehnheiligen, with Holtzendorf and Rüchel attacking on other parts of the field; these are main attacks by each side, not counterattacks inside a defended position. The accounts agree on the code, so they are one claim. Napoleon decided to attack from the Landgrafenberg (claim napoleon-decision), the prince to advance on Vierzehnheiligen and Rüchel to attack from Kapellendorf (claim side-b-command), so the posture is tagged commander_created. Foucart notes that the Bulletin passes over the last combat of the day, at Capellendorf against Rüchel's corps, as it does over the opening combat at Closwitz against Tauentzien's, and that the French centre's second attack was directed on Vierzehnheiligen, not on Hohlstedt as the Bulletin has it (OCR). English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'it was ... o'clock in the morning when Napoleon gave the order to attack,'; 'and at about the same time General Count Tauentzien ordered that the troops under him should reoccupy the position held the evening before, which they had left in the night as a precaution'; 'through this advance on both sides the fighting parties very soon ran into each other'; as in claim side-b-command for the heading of the opening fight, the advance and the echelons, and in claim side-a-command for Napoleon's defensive; the heading of the third moment, 'the French are reinforced by the troops of Marshals Soult and Augereau, the division Marchand of Ney's corps and by cavalry, and renew the attack'; 'the moment was missed, and so the whole mass of fresh forces now at last pressed forward against the Prussian troops thinned and shaken by a fire of several hours'; as in claim side-b-command for Holtzendorf's attack and Rüchel's attack and advance; 'the advancing troops are outflanked and enfiladed by new enemy lines' (OCR); Suchet, as in claim side-a-losses-reported for the heading and date; '... at daybreak I formed the brigade Claparède in line of battle, followed by 2 pieces, to seize the small village of Closwitz, which lay on our right, the brigade in two lines, the artillery in the intervals' (p. 632); the Bulletin, as in claim foucart-side-a for the heading and date (p. 614); 'however good the position the enemy occupied, he was dislodged from it, and the French army, debouching into the plain, began to take its order of battle' (OCR); as in claim side-b-objectives for the enemy's plan and in claim foucart-side-b for the two corps (p. 617); 'several battalions having engaged at the village of Hohlstedt, he saw the enemy set off to dislodge them from it; Marshal Lannes received the order at once to march in echelons to support this village'; Foucart's note, 'the second attack of the centre of the French army was directed on the village of Vierzehn-Heiligen, and not on the village of Hohlstädt. It was the Emperor himself who ordered this attack. (Report of General Suchet.)'; as in claim side-a-command for the reserves and the first line; 'the bulletin no more speaks of the last combat of the day, that of Capellendorf, against the corps of General Rüchel, than it dwelt at the start of the battle on the combat of Closwitz against the corps of General Tauenzien' (OCR).

claims.value: No passage read has either side fight from works. At Vierzehnheiligen the French held behind houses and barns against the fire of the battery Wolframsdorf, and, when they left the front houses, still held behind the garden enclosures as before, so that only the bayonet could have helped; Napoleon held the village although it was burning (OCR). The left of the French army rested on a village and woods (the 5th Bulletin). In the Bulletin the enemy defended the road from Jena to Weimar 'in force and by an impregnable position', without naming works.
claims.rationale: Code none_named: the places held were a village with its houses, barns and garden enclosures, woods and a plateau, held without named works. A coding that counted the garden enclosures ('Befriedigungen der Gärten', which the passages read do not describe as walls) as walls would give A_fortified for the French at Vierzehnheiligen. The Bulletin's 'impregnable position' names no works. The accounts agree on the code, so they are one claim, and a none_named code takes the phase unresolved; none_named reports the passages read, not proof that no works existed. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'the mighty fire of the battery Wolframsdorf could not win possession of the village, since the enemy held behind houses and barns'; 'the French left the front houses, but held behind the enclosures of the gardens as before, and the further throwing of incendiary shells was soon stopped. Only the bayonet could have helped here'; as in claim side-a-command for Napoleon's defensive (OCR); the Bulletin, as in claim foucart-side-a for the heading and date (p. 614); as in claim napoleon-decision for the road from Jena to Weimar (p. 615); as in claim side-a-command for the left (p. 617).

open_questions: Deferred: in Foucart, the Jena documents between the 5th Bulletin and his tables, read in the OCR in the targeted follow-up or in search snippets, of which only General Suchet's report is selected and cited: General Victor's report as chief of staff of the 5th corps (from p. 625) and the extract of Lieutenant-Colonel von der Goltz's account that follows it (pp. 630-632); General Foucher's report on the 5th corps's artillery (p. 635); the journal of the 4th corps (pp. 636-642), which ends with a loss for the division Saint-Hilaire and the cavalry; General Lariboisière's report on that corps's artillery (from p. 642); Marshal Soult's letter to the major general (pp. 643-645); Marshal Ney's letters to the Emperor (pp. 645-650), one giving a loss for his advanced guard; the report of the 6th corps's artillery (p. 650); Marshal Augereau's letters to the major general (pp. 651 and 665) and reports of regiments and artillery of the 7th corps (pp. 657-664), several with unit losses; General d'Hautpoul's report to the grand-duc de Berg (p. 667); Colonel Blein's account beyond Foucart's note on p. 619; the 5th Bulletin's text on p. 616 and pp. 618-619, read in the OCR (cited only as marked); and Foucart's tables of the troops that would have arrived had the King's army not moved on Naumburg (p. 671, not transcribed). In Höpfner, his plan of Jena and his Beilage D, an extract of General Rüchel's dispositions, not inspected; p. 428, on Marshal Bernadotte's corps, read in the OCR at the batch check and not cited. Figures read only in the OCR are not restated: among them the hours of the day, the Guard infantry on the Landgrafenberg, Holtzendorf's detachment, the French force at the time of the prince's advance, and the losses of the Gettkandt hussars, the regiment Winning and the French units in the documents above.

Most consequential gap: side A's losses at Jena. The 5th Bulletin's 1,000 or 1,100 killed and 3,000 wounded cover Jena and Auerstedt together; General Suchet's 2,645 with 75 officers are for his division and may include Saalfeld; Bodart's about 6,000 with 333 officers has no source in the passages read; Höpfner finds no credible figure. The targeted follow-up searched the OCR of Foucart's Jena documents (pp. 621-668) for 'pertes' (12 hits: pp. 629, 632 twice, 636, 640, 644 twice, 645, 651, 653, 658 and 668) and 'tués' (24 hits: pp. 635 three times, 642 twice, 643 three times, 644, 645, 646, 650, 651 twice, 653, 655, 657, 658, 659, 661 twice, 662, 663 and 664), read each hit in its snippet, read pp. 625 and 629-636, 642, 646 and 650 in the OCR, and selected and transcribed General Suchet's report (pp. 632-635). The hits are mostly losses of single regiments, batteries and teams, the Prussians' losses in von der Goltz's account, a circular from Ulrichshalben asking the divisions for returns of their losses by regiment (p. 644) and a report whose writer did not yet have the return of losses (p. 668); besides Suchet's, the only larger French totals found are the 4th corps's journal for the division Saint-Hilaire and the cavalry (p. 642) and Marshal Ney's loss for his advanced guard (p. 650), both read only in the OCR. No return for the French army at Jena was found. Transcribing those two passages and Marshal Augereau's reports from their page images could narrow the gap but would not give a total.

Disputes recorded in the claims: side A's strength (Bodart 72 battalions, 75 squadrons, 108 guns and 96,000 men, 54,000 in action; Foucart's tables 82 battalions, 83,600 men, 75 squadrons and 12,300 horses, 95,900 in all (our arithmetic), with several divisions present but not engaged; the 5th Bulletin 3,000 men for Ney against the table's 3,400 men and 1,100 horses); side B's strength (Bodart 54,000 with 17,000 Saxons; Höpfner some 50,000; Goltz 40,000 for Hohenlohe and 15,000 for Rüchel; Foucart's estimates 44,000 and 28,000 including the Duke of Weimar's advanced guard; the 5th Bulletin 80,000 for the two corps before Jena; the later Bulletin 126,000 for both fields; Lannes's estimate about 50,000); the French loss (the 5th Bulletin 1,000 or 1,100 killed and 3,000 wounded for both fields; Suchet 2,645 with 75 officers for his division, perhaps with Saalfeld; Bodart about 6,000 with 333 officers; Höpfner no credible figure); side B's loss (the 5th Bulletin 30,000 to 40,000 prisoners, more than 20,000 killed or wounded, 300 pieces of cannon and 25 to 30 colours for both fields; Bodart about 12,000 killed and wounded, 15,000 prisoners and 112 cannon; Höpfner 312 officers (our arithmetic) and 24 Prussian guns without the battalion guns, the men's loss not to be stated); and the French centre's second attack (the 5th Bulletin Hohlstedt; Foucart's note, from Suchet's report, Vierzehnheiligen). Also noted: Bodart's printed 11·0%, 22·3%, 27·7% and 65% against 11·1%, 22·2%, 27·8% and 64% (our arithmetic).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his side B officers' losses, 312 with 9 generals and 46 staff officers, and his Saxon officers, 114 with 15 staff officers, equal Höpfner's, all by our arithmetic; by his note his side B losses in men come from French sources (Martin); his French strengths are close to Foucart's tables; the passages read do not show what he used for the French losses or the Saxon strength); Foucart (the French staff edition of 1887, printing the 5th Bulletin and a later Bulletin of the Grande Armée, General Suchet's report and other French reports, with notes quoting Colonel Blein and Lieutenant-Colonel von der Goltz, and his own tables and estimates); Höpfner (the Prussian history of 1850, which gives Napoleon's disposition and address in German without naming its source in the passages read). Goltz's account is quoted in French by Foucart; the passages read do not name the work or show whether it shares sources with Höpfner. The 5th Bulletin is Napoleon's own account; Suchet's report is a separate French document in the same edition.
